title: Architecture Decision Records
description: Learn to capture and communicate architecture decisions with lightweight ADRs. Understand when to write them, what sections matter, and how to use ADRs to align teams and preserve context.

data.text: Every nontrivial system is shaped by decisions: why this database, why this framework, why this deployment model. The problem is that these decisions are often made in a meeting, partially documented, and then forgotten. Six months later, a new team member asks why the system uses Message Bus X instead of Queue Y, and nobody remembers the original reasoning. **Architecture Decision Records, or ADRs**, exist to prevent that.

An ADR is a short document that captures a single significant decision, the context around it, and the consequences. It is not a design document, a requirements spec, or a tutorial. It is a historical artifact that answers the question: 'Here is what we decided, here is why, and here is what changed because of it.'

data.title: Key ADR concepts
items: Decision: The specific choice the team made.
Context: The forces and constraints that made the decision nontrivial.
Consequences: The outcomes of the decision, both positive and negative.
Status: Whether the decision is proposed, accepted, deprecated, or superseded.
Superseded By: A reference to a later ADR that replaces this one, creating an audit trail.

data.text: A good ADR is short enough that people actually write it. The classic template, popularized by Michael Nygard, has five sections: title, status, context, decision, and consequences. You can store ADRs as Markdown files in your repository so they live alongside the code they describe.

data.title: ADR-001: Use PostgreSQL for transactional data
data.content: A complete ADR written as a Markdown file in an docs/adr/ folder.
data.code:
# ADR-001: Use PostgreSQL for transactional data

## Status
Accepted

## Context
We need a durable relational store for orders, customers, and
payments. The team has experience with SQL Server, but we are
deploying to Azure and want to reduce licensing cost. We also
need JSON support for flexible product attributes.

## Decision
Use PostgreSQL on Azure Database for PostgreSQL as the primary
transactional store. Use EF Core as the data access layer.

## Consequences
### Positive
- No SQL Server licensing cost.
- Strong JSONB support for product attributes.
- Managed PostgreSQL reduces operational overhead.

### Negative
- Team needs to learn PostgreSQL-specific tuning.
- EF Core provider for PostgreSQL is less mature than SQL Server.
- Existing internal tools assume SQL Server.

## Superseded By
- ADR-003: Migrate to Azure SQL for managed identity support

data.text: Not every decision deserves an ADR. ADRs are for decisions that are hard to reverse, expensive to change, or likely to be questioned later. Good candidates include choosing a database, adopting a cloud provider, selecting a messaging technology, or defining a cross-cutting pattern such as authentication. A trivial choice like naming a variable or choosing a NuGet package for logging does not need an ADR.

data.title: ADR scope signals
data.text: If a decision affects more than one team, requires nontrivial migration work, or locks you into a vendor or framework, write an ADR. If the decision is reversible in an afternoon, skip the ADR and leave a code comment instead.
Using ADRs in a C# Codebase

In a C# project, keep ADRs in a dedicated `docs/adr/` folder at the repository root. Name them with a sequential number and short slug, such as `0001-use-postgresql.md`. Use consistent front matter or headings so teammates can scan the list quickly. If you use GitHub, ADRs work well as pull request descriptions that are merged into the main branch and preserved in git history.

data.title: Mistakes to avoid
items: Writing the ADR after the decision is already implemented and treated as a justification rather than a record.
Leaving the ADR status as 'Accepted' forever even when the decision is later reversed.
Skipping the Consequences section, which is where the real trade-offs live.
Storing ADRs in a wiki that does not travel with the code repository.

terms.definition: Architecture Decision Record: a short document that captures a significant decision, its context, and its consequences.
An older ADR that was replaced by a newer decision. It should remain in the repository for historical context.
The complete collection of ADRs for a project or organization.

data.title: Write an ADR for your current project
data.description: Identify one architecture decision in your current project and document it as an ADR.
steps: Pick a decision that was hard to reverse or that new team members often question.
Create a new Markdown file in docs/adr/ with a sequential number.
Write the context: what forces, constraints, or requirements led to this decision?
Write the decision: what exactly did the team decide to do?
Write the consequences: what became easier, and what became harder?
Set the status to Accepted and commit the ADR.
data.expectedOutcome: A short, honest ADR that future teammates can read to understand why the system is built the way it is.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: ADRs capture the 'why' behind architecture decisions in a lightweight, readable format.
Good ADRs are short, honest, and include consequences, not justifications.
Store ADRs in the repository alongside the code they describe.
Supersede old ADRs instead of deleting them to preserve decision history.
data.takeaway: Architecture decisions are as important as the code they shape. Documenting them with ADRs turns tribal knowledge into institutional knowledge.
